comments.name: Ann Grant
comments.body:
I started quilting in my late 50's.  I learned from a group of hand quilters.  I have three hand-quilted queen bed sized quilts which I rotate annually on my bed.  Relatives got wedding, anniversary,and baby quilts.  Friends because I felt like it.  Foster kids one year got 11.  Meals on Wheels got over 300 placemats from our small quilt grip of six.   You do the math.

I always have a couple of charity quilts ready to go for the inevitable Colorado wildfire.  I had to quit hand quilting about 12 years ago due to arthritis in my thumbs so now machine and free motion quilt.  I have downsized and moved into art quilting.  I only have domestic machines, a small one for traveling and an old Singer which was a wedding present from my father-in-law who was an engineer at Singer.  It has metal gears, no belts, no computer boards to go out, and I maintain it myself as most repair shops won't touch it.  I have a PhD in chemistry and operated ma as spectrometers during my career, the first instruments similarly not computerized.

Sewing, gardening, baking sourdough and from scratch are all satisfying occupations which provide a state of flow during the creation and a product which is tangible and rewarding.

comments.name: Pat Shediack

I retired in December 2022 after 46 years of work with 44 of that as a supervisor of some kind or another and 39 as a project manager in various business, technical or government areas.  I also earned my master of science in management specializing in project management as well as the global PM certification.  Three years into retirement, I'm still receiving inquiries from companies about interviewing with them.  

When I read the job descriptions I'm sent I see a grocery list of requirements that literally no one I ever encountered in the PM field could meet--including me.  It's pretty obvious the job requirements are nothing more than a hiring manager's list of "I wants", "I'd like" and "It would be great if we could get someone who also do X, Y or Z".  HR then plugged into various data entry fields in their AI-based recruiting system which screened the incoming resumes.  In short, the company is looking for a unicorn.    

If hiring managers are looking for "unicorns", they're on a fool's mission.  The HR managers and staff helping them search for those "unicorns" are just as foolish.  

For those job seekers who can't seem to break through the AI resume screening system, try some other things like joining whatever professional society, trade group or business group relates to your field, go in the military or apply for public service or non-profit jobs.  Make a grocery list of every single skill you have, then apply to global, national & local firms who use those skills.

While no movie can ever encapsulate a work of such vast complexity and nuance, Nolan achieves something monumental. He dispenses with entire episodes (Nausikaa), collapses others into one, and glosses over or erases entire scenes, but in remaining true to his own vision, he does Homer full justice.  I loved how he kept returning to the Trojan War as an instigating and destructive force. 

A few quibbles that don't feel minor:

If you include the Polyphemus/Cyclops episode, as you must, why drop the most spectacular part of it—the “Nobody” trick? The Greeks saw it as Odysseus’s greatest stratagem after the Trojan horse. It captures his fatal complexity perfectly: clever enough to tell Polyphemus his name is “Nobody,” which saves the crew when the Cyclops cries that “Nobody” is hurting him, yet arrogant enough, once safely at sea, to taunt him and announce his real name, lineage, and kingdom. That single burst of hubris is what dooms them; it is the moment Poseidon turns against Odysseus.

Why leave out the harrowing moment when Helen walks past the Trojan horse, hears the men whispering inside, and faces an impossible choice? She can betray Odysseus's men or save them by keeping their secret and, in doing so, betray her adopted country of Troy. She chooses the latter, leaving her with as much blood on her hands as Odysseus. She puns that she calls Troy "Destroy."

Despite those misses, Nolan’s own vision is cohesive, compelling, and devastating. He's reanimated a lost world.

We wanted that as much as the buyer did.  Being a landlord, or tenant, with no contractual agreement as to each parties duties and responsibilities isn't sound business or real estate practice.  Every thing worked out in our post-sale possession for us and the buyer, but a negotiated rental agreement is essential to increase the potential for that outcome.  Closing in this situation and hoping for the best can lead to some very difficult, and expensive to remediate, consequences.

We bought our home in December '99. The sellers were building their dream home in Orange County. They wanted to rent back to us for 6 mos while their home was being built.  We were first time home buyers and were living in an apartment we loved. We were bidding against a family that had a larger down payment than we did. My husband calculated the rent  they would charge the seller for the competing family.  
We offered them a lower rent than the other family and they took our bid even though our down payment was smaller. (But the price they were selling it for was the same for both parties) We had a well written contract and everything went pretty smoothly. But there is no way I would rent back without a valid contract.  We assumed they would be keeping their gardeners.  They didn't and the yard was very overgrown.  We would have happily paid for the gardener but they didn't even give us the opportunity to pay them.

In fact, a lot of the listing sheets said "Possession 30 (or more) days after closing." I assured her, "I'm not from these parts," and I do business differently. If the seller needs more time to move out, we can simply have a later closing date, I'm flexible. But the day of the closing, we do a walk through, I get the keys, and adios to the sellers. Some hurt feelings, but they came around.

Years ago I lived in Hawaii and tourists would regularly ask me, sotto voce, where the 'secret' beaches were. I would look them in the eye and reply that if I told them, they wouldn't be secret, now would they? They were always kind of shocked.

It's worse now. I live in Africa, and we have a very large private wildlife reserve, which is unfenced so as not to impede natural wildlife migrations. We are regularly finding people 'wild camping' on the land, thanks to an app called iOverlander that posts fabulous spots to 'wild camp', AKA trespass, on private land.

I've contacted the app and demanded they remove the designations. I've rated it and complained to the App Store and will continue to do so.
Because of major wildfire and poaching problems, camping outside of designated areas is illegal in this country, and there are three commercial campsites within 10 kms of these illegal sites. It would cost tens of thousands of dollars to re-fence the land, money that currently goes to conservation projects. We will no longer be polite when asking people to pack up and leave. The entitlement of tourists is breathtaking.

This is one of the most ironic things I’ve noticed when this and related subjects come up. The “gatekeepers” and activists so often only sit on a residency timeline slightly longer than the tourists themselves. I surmise it’s because unlike born-and-raised locals, they are often well-enough-off gentrifiers who can afford to live without tourists and want to keep their hotspots - typically operated by born-and-raised locals, who see the tourists as a boon - cheap and quiet for themselves.

It is certainly true in my own regional vacation destination - the schoolteachers who could afford waterfront homes have long since been driven away, replaced by second homeowners or well-off remote workers, retirees and artists who complain about the tourists. I don’t have a problem with new residents anywhere - for years I was one in NYC - but the entitlement and lack of self-awareness drives me nuts.

Great, you moved there eight years ago and now want to cut off access. Sounds like the immigrants who got here forty years ago and now want to turn away others.  The only constant is change.  Your little town, is going to change.  It won’t be what it was when you were young, it won’t be what it was ten years ago.  Accept that reality or keep trying to hold back the tide.  Find a way to live in peace with it, regulate it for moderation but you will lose against the people of the world.  Tourists can be annoying, but having grown up in a tourist town in a tourist state, those people pay a steep price to visit and kept us from paying taxes.  Sure, the spring break crowds got out of hand in the 1980s and we nudged them to other places that were desperate for their money…but don’t kill the golden goose of tourism, learn to live with it.

Yes, some US tourists are loud and maybe rude.  Once in Vienna, while a docent was discussing aspects of the architecture, one  American lady spied a Starbucks, yelled its name and went running to it coming back with...Starbucks coffee.  Rude, yes but also stupid.  With many beautiful coffee houses, why? In Trieste, Italy, we were having pizza  and a bottle of wine in a small restaurant .  The young lady was having trouble opening the bottle with a waiters corkscrew (who doesn't??) and my wife and I were saying some encouraging words to her.  She finally got it and I told her my problems with those cork screws.  When I was paying the bill, the owner asked me if I was American.  I replied "yes" and he said "You're not like the other Americans," who he believed were rude and demanding.  Politeness and patience will always win the day.

I am a lucky guy. I've been to CDMX three times in less than a year and a half. This is a vibrant, alive and intriguing place to which I would prefer to go if I were 24 again rather than camping out in Paris, as I did reflexly at that age, burdened by too much reading about its romantic character and filled with literary hopefulness. Mexico City is an happening place, maybe the place.

Don't go there. Your huddled masses  yearning to breathe free, with considerable effort, are going to maybe ruin it, if it can be ruined. I am not telling you about my favorite neighborhoods, nor the spectacular museums, nor the relentlessly expressive, random artistic thrusts of the population, nor the kind, welcoming people I met, nor the cab drivers who can be hired for a few dollars an hour, nor the skating contests and community workouts  and real life I saw in Pushkin Park. No, none of that.

Hey, if you go, take off your tourist attitude vibes and dip in deeply. Learn something, learn a lot. Eat from street vendors the way perhaps 60% of the population does at lunch time, and where one taco seller won a MICHELIN Star last year. Go to all those museums and discover for yourself.

It is a friendly city with temporary and long term ex-pats approachable and generally eager to talk. A different place. Come back and don't tell anyone about it other than to smile when it is mentioned. Buy some of my photo artworks, too, if they are on display.

comments.name: Mary Sweeney
comments.body:
I recall reading that Laura Ingalls Wilder initially set out to write an adult version of her life on the prairie. But her publisher (and I think her daughter Rose) decided that a children's book would sell better. (I have to wonder if there was sexism involved as the idea of a woman writing a much tougher and more accurate story of life on the prairie might not have gone over well.) At the time the family really needed money and Laura went with the children's version. 

Much as I enjoyed the Little House books as a child, I really wish Laura had written the adult version. I think we lost a lot when she didn't. And the books she did write added to a highly romantized version of "going west" that continues to shape our nation's mythology today, sometimes in unfortunate ways and I'm not talking just about racism. For one thing, Pa Ingalls' restless insistence on pulling up stakes as soon as communities began to form in what used to be frontier made for a lot of adventure but also kept the family in poverty. It really does take a village, something we like to forget with the emphasis we place on rugged individualism.

comments.name: Chris K

Ironic timing. While Germany debates dismantling its Sunday shopping ban, hundreds of thousands of soccer fans flying into the New York area today for the World Cup Final will run headfirst into America's own version of it.

The stadium is in Bergen County, NJ, where Spain and Argentina play for the trophy this afternoon. Bergen County also happens to enforce some of the strictest blue laws left in the U.S.: general merchandise sales are banned on Sundays. 

Bergen County has some of the largest retail complexes in the country, magnets for exactly the kind of international tourist traffic a World Cup Final brings, will have their clothing, electronics, and furniture sections effectively closed to shoppers, by state statute that dates to the 1950s.

So a Spanish fan wanting to buy a jersey after the match, or an Argentine visitor needing a jacket for the cold front behind those two goals, will discover that "sacred Sunday" isn't just a German constitutional quirk, it's also across the Hudson River from Times Square. Restaurants, bars, and the stadium concessions will be running at full tilt, of course; it's only retail that stops. A fitting real-world footnote to the WSJ piece: even the country that invented Black Friday still has a Sonntagsruhe of its own, tucked into the New Jersey suburbs, on the single busiest tourism day of the year.

The fact that China can produce state-of-the-art (SOTA) models, particularly for long-horizon agentic tasks, and is willing to give them away for free, means it will be very hard for OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google to convince customers to pay a premium for their models. Since open source models can be hosted by anyone, the market will drive down the cost of AI to marginal cost--which makes frontier AI a commodity. That is bad news for Silicon Valley, but in the long run, it is good news for the economy. It prevents Silicon Valley from charging high rents on their AI models and capturing for themselves the value of the productivity benefits that AI creates. That means that AI adoption will be accelerated and AI technology will diffuse faster to the overall economy than would otherwise be the case. And AI adoption and diffusion is the #1 driver of future productivity growth, which is essential to the health and wealth of the U.S economy. Therefore, the Chinese are really doing us a favor. The growing frustration with public officials leveraging their office for personal or political gain points to a deeper, structural failure. The presidential pardon.(Article II, Section 2), is functionally absolute and a relic modeled after the British "royal prerogative of mercy." Hamilton argued that a single executive needed this power for swift execution during national crises. Instead, it has evolved into a tool for political cronyism and self-preservation, completely unchecked by Congress or the judiciary.

A rational system would treat this power as a high-stakes legal exception, perhaps requiring a unanimous Supreme Court recommendation or explicit legislative approval before a pardon is finalized. By making the amendment process practically impossible in a polarized era, we have frozen the rules of the game in 1787. If we cannot find a way to structurally check absolute powers like the pardon, we shouldn't be surprised when those powers are inevitably abused.  (Written with the aid of Gemini... ideas are mine)

Ah some bat love! Bats are so fantastic... 
As someone with a zoonotic disease focus I really want folks to understand that the most efficient way to control mosquito populations, and the vector-borne diseases they carry, is the way nature intended - mosquito predators.
And bats are the best at catching them - one bat might consume on average 1000-3000 mosquitoes per night, the little brown bat even up to 1200 every hour.
Welcome every bat you see, it may just save your life, if it catches the exact mosquito that would have infected you with a vector-borne disease that would have made you really, really sick...
For me, every bat is a little Batman, instead of fighting crime, fighting these serious and debilitating diseases, Malaria, Dengue, Chikungunya, Zika, Yellow Fever, West Nile, Japanese Encephalitis...
Oh, and they reforest tropical forests, disperse seeds and fertilize as well - the Max Planck Institute in Radolfzell (with colleagues from Sweden and Ghana), have calculated the ecological/financial benefits of straw-coloured fruit bats in Africa. So, every night, these bats fly long distances to their feeding grounds, which means they disseminate the seeds of the fruits they consume. So, 150,000 animals disseminate more than 300,000 small seeds in a single night. This is sufficient to kickstart the regrowth of 800 hectares of forest -  the animals of one single bat colony...!

All the small businesses in their area suffered extensive damage - sports gear and cycling shops, television and video gear, our regional healthcare system’s urgent care location. After last year’s disaster, I’d returned to the joy of cycling our River Trail to grocery, yoga, church - leaving my car in the garage. Now I struggle to comprehend the stunning losses of friends whose homes near to creeks are flooded for the first time, neighbors on my street next to the river flooded for the second time in a year and 13 days, and the loss of our magnificent lifestyle. I just adopted a lab whose great joy was daily off-leash runs at the county dog park along the river - she’s frantic with unreleased energy in the last two days without access to the destroyed park. And my feral cat colony that I sustained for over three years along the creek bed meadow across the street - the cats survived but their meadow and all the trees, wildflowers were washed away. The feral cats are now in our street, challenging domesticated cats for territory, afraid of the human they once allowed to pet them as they fed on their limestone ledge overlooking the creek. Repeated flooding changes everything in our lives. Beauty is gone for now.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
We are experiencing a very non linear increase of local and regional climate-related impacts surprising many scientists by how soon they are occurring: heat waves, droughts, wildfires, floods, stronger storms, etc.

This is in large part because ice melt, which reduces heat reflectivity, is causing the Arctic to warm around 4 times the rate of the whole planet and the decreased horizontal temperature gradient between the Arctic and the rest of the world has helped cause the northern polar jet stream to slow, and get stuck in wavy patterns.

These patterns bleed heat north and cold south, and cause weather systems to persist (like the heat wave that spread fire that incinerated Lytton, British Columbia a few years ago).

Also for every degree C rise in temperature the atmosphere can hold 7 percent more moisture, an exponential increase. Hence the “rain bombs” we’ve been seeing around the world.

As we get flooded by this from above the rate of sea level rise is accelerating and maximum storm strength is increasing.

There’s some adapting that we have to do to the changes already in the pipeline, but it wouldn’t take us long to make the changes too big to adapt to.
